entities.summary: Aequian is an extinct Italic language presumed spoken by the people the Romans termed Aequi and Aequicoli living in the Alban Hills of northeast Latium and the central Apennines east of them during the early and middle Roman Republic; that is, approximately from the 5th to the 3rd century BC, when they were defeated by the armies of Rome and were subsequently Romanized. As the area was heavily colonized by Latin speakers from Rome, most of the inscriptions from there are in Latin. Two undated inscriptions appear to be in a different dialect, termed Aequian by the scholars with the presumption that in fact they represent the language of the entire pre-Roman tribe.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: The Aequian language played a crucial role in shaping the early Roman Republic, with its speakers being defeated and subsequently assimilated into Latin-speaking populations. The study of Aequian provides valuable insights into the linguistic and cultural dynamics of ancient Italy.
